title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 35–36
description: Advanced vocabulary for border controls, police procedures and digital crime, followed by beliefs, argumentation, ideological word families and expressions of certainty.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied book. Vocabulary targets and use distinctions were checked against the source units, exercises and answer key. Translations, examples and explanatory notes were independently written; original textbook passages and exercises are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 35 teaching sections A–C, numbered glosses, the plural-police warning, exercises 35.1–35.4 and answer key; Unit 36 teaching sections A–C, definitions and word-family table, exercises 36.1–36.4 and answer key.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA provided selectively where reasonably confident. Empty IPA means no reliable transcription was established; longer expressions may omit IPA. Text-to-speech voices and pronunciation were not evaluated.
audit.languagePolicy: Learner-facing content and metadata are English; Brazilian Portuguese appears only in pt fields.
audit.reviewMethod: Checked the supplied PDF study and exercise pages, page images, word-family table and relevant answer key; wrote independent examples and usage notes, then validated JSON schema parity, unique IDs, source metadata, item types and static Word/Sentence TTS targets.
audit.limitations: The package includes no recorded MP3s. VocabLab browser importing, TTS voice behaviour and pronunciation recognition have not been tested. Country-specific legal and immigration rules are not presented as current guidance.

units.title: Unit 35 — Authorities: customs and police
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 76–77 (PDF pages 78–79).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Government and law · border formalities, policing and cybercrime
learningObjectives: Use border-control vocabulary accurately, including customs declarations, allowances, identity checks and entry requirements.
Distinguish refugees, asylum-seekers and the formal action of claiming asylum while avoiding assumptions about national regulations.
Use policing and traffic-enforcement collocations in context, including enforce the law, stop and search and search warrant.
Describe security roles and digital offences precisely, distinguishing plain-clothes police from undercover officers and phishing from wider cybercrime.

sectionsChecked: A · Entering a country, numbered explanations and terminology
B · Policing the streets and surveillance vocabulary
C · Other types of policing, cybersecurity terminology and Common mistakes

items.pt: cartão de desembarque; formulário de chegada
items.example: Passengers filled in a landing card before reaching passport control.
items.note: A form recording arrival and personal details; requirements vary by country.

items.example: She completed a customs declaration form to report the goods in her luggage.
items.note: A declaration of goods or money brought across a border, rather than an application for a visa.

items.example: He checked whether his visa permitted multiple entries.
items.note: Official permission relating to entry or stay; the rules depend on the destination.

items.example: The tour operator advised travellers to carry a vaccination certificate.
items.note: Evidence of relevant vaccinations; it is not the same as a medical prescription.

items.example: Before booking, they read the entry regulations for foreign visitors.
items.note: Formal rules about who may enter a country and under what conditions.

items.pt: portões eletrônicos de controle de passaportes
items.example: Eligible passengers went through the e-passport gates after landing.
items.note: Automated border gates that verify eligible travel documents and sometimes biometric data.

items.example: The checkpoint uses facial recognition technology to compare images.
items.note: A technical noun phrase referring to automated face identification or verification.

items.example: A customs officer asked whether she had anything to declare.
items.note: An official who checks goods entering a country; not interchangeable with an immigration officer.

items.example: Officers carried out spot checks on randomly selected bags.
items.note: Spot checks examine selected cases rather than checking every person or item.

items.example: Customs staff confiscated several banned goods at the border.
items.note: Banned means prohibited altogether in the relevant context.

items.example: Travellers should declare restricted goods before leaving the inspection area.
items.note: Restricted means permitted only within conditions or limits, unlike outright banned.

items.example: She stayed within her customs allowance when buying gifts abroad.
items.note: The legally permitted quantity or value; go over your allowance means exceed it.

items.example: He had to pay additional duty after going over his allowance.
items.note: Go over means exceed a permitted limit; the source uses it for goods brought across borders.

items.example: Sniffer dogs were deployed to inspect incoming parcels.
items.note: Trained to find particular substances by smell; detector dogs is an alternative term.

items.example: Detector dogs searched the cargo area for prohibited materials.
items.note: An alternative to sniffer dogs in the book's customs context.

items.example: The scanner can detect substances hidden inside the package.
items.note: Detect involves finding or identifying something, often not immediately visible.

items.pt: passar pela alfândega; concluir a inspeção alfandegária
items.example: We cleared customs before collecting the keys to our hire car.
items.note: A fixed travel expression; clear is a verb here, not an adjective meaning transparent.

items.pt: ponto oficial de entrada no país
items.example: The form asks you to identify your first port of entry.
items.note: May refer to an authorised airport or other border crossing, not just a seaport.

items.example: The charity provides temporary housing for refugees.
items.note: A person who has fled their country; legal definitions may involve specific protection criteria.

items.example: The family decided to claim asylum after fleeing persecution.
items.note: A formal expression meaning request protection in another country; an application does not itself guarantee status.

items.pt: solicitante de asilo; pessoa que pede refúgio
items.example: The legal clinic explained the process to an asylum-seeker.
items.note: A person seeking protection; distinct from someone whose claim has already been formally recognised.

items.example: She described years of persecution because of her political views.
items.note: Serious mistreatment based on identity or beliefs, not merely criticism or inconvenience.

items.example: The authorities are responsible for enforcing the law fairly.
items.note: Enforce means make sure rules are obeyed; do not confuse it with force a law.

items.example: Officers must follow the relevant rules when they stop and search someone.
items.note: A coordinated pair of verbs; lawful powers and safeguards differ between jurisdictions.

items.example: The package raised suspicion during the inspection.
items.note: The belief that something may be wrong without certainty or proof.

items.example: Investigators discovered stolen property in the abandoned vehicle.
items.note: Property used as a collective noun for possessions; theft and robbery are not identical offences.

items.example: The detectives obtained a search warrant before entering the flat.
items.note: An official authorisation to search; exact requirements depend on the legal system.

items.pt: radar de velocidade; câmera de fiscalização de velocidade
items.example: A speed camera recorded vehicles travelling above the limit.
items.note: Used to identify possible speeding violations.

items.example: The driver was fined for exceeding the speed limit.
items.note: A formal construction; speeding is a shorter noun for the offence.

items.example: A traffic warden issued a ticket to the parked car.
items.note: British term for an official dealing with parking enforcement; job titles vary elsewhere.

items.example: A warden issued a parking ticket after the car had been left on double yellow lines.
items.note: Issue is a formal verb meaning officially give or produce a notice or document.

items.example: She appealed against the parking fine using photographs.
items.note: A fine is the monetary penalty; a ticket is the notice recording the alleged infringement.

items.example: The station expanded its surveillance system in the ticket hall.
items.note: A formal word for systematic observation, often for security or investigation.

items.example: CCTV footage helped investigators establish the sequence of events.
items.note: Closed-circuit television; the initials are spoken separately.

items.example: The cameras monitor public areas near the transport hub.
items.note: Monitor as a verb means observe or check regularly; public area is a common noun phrase.

items.example: The security forces coordinated their response to the incident.
items.note: A collective label that can include police and military bodies, depending on context.

items.example: Plain-clothes police observed the suspect without wearing uniforms.
items.note: Describes officers dressed in ordinary clothes; they need not be operating under a false identity.

items.example: An undercover police officer entered the organisation under an assumed identity.
items.note: Undercover refers to concealed identity or covert work, not merely the absence of a uniform.

items.pt: unidade policial de combate ao tráfico de drogas
items.example: The drug squad investigated a network of illegal suppliers.
items.note: A specialised police unit; squad here means a team.

items.example: The anti-corruption squad opened an inquiry into the payment scheme.
items.note: A team investigating dishonest or corrupt conduct, including bribery.

items.pt: suborno; prática de oferecer ou receber propina
items.example: The official faced allegations of bribery connected with public contracts.
items.note: The giving or receiving of inducements to influence behaviour improperly.

items.example: The report describes measures designed to prevent corruption.
items.note: A broad term for abuse of entrusted power, not restricted to a single payment.

items.example: The bank trained staff to recognise signs of cybercrime.
items.note: Umbrella term for crimes involving computer systems or networks.

items.example: The seminar discussed the risks associated with cyberterrorism.
items.note: A specialised term referring to terrorism involving digital systems; not a synonym for ordinary cybercrime.

items.example: The analysis distinguishes cyberwarfare from financially motivated attacks.
items.note: A term for hostile operations involving digital systems in a conflict context.

items.pt: golpe de phishing; fraude para roubar dados por mensagens falsas
items.example: A phishing message tried to persuade employees to reveal their passwords.
items.note: Fraudulent attempts to obtain confidential information by pretending to be trustworthy.

items.pt: a polícia (substantivo coletivo com concordância plural em inglês)
items.example: The police are investigating several reports of online fraud.
items.note: In standard English, the police normally takes a plural verb: the police are, not the police is.

items.example: Please keep your declaration ready when you reach customs control.
items.note: Refers to official checks of goods at a border; not the same as passport control.

items.example: The guidance explains which infectious diseases require additional precautions.
items.note: A disease caused by an infectious agent; the phrase appears in the exercise about vaccination certificates.

units.title: Unit 36 — Beliefs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 78–79 (PDF pages 80–81).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Beliefs and arguments · viewpoints, persuasion, judgement and certainty
learningObjectives: Describe supporters and opponents of beliefs, preserving the connotations and grammar of related word families.
Discuss pacifism and public advocacy using accurate terms such as tenet, proponent, derive from and civil disobedience.
Distinguish credible from incredulous, plausible from implausible, and subjective from objective.
Use idioms and patterns for uncertainty and attribution, including presume, benefit of the doubt and take something with a pinch of salt.

sectionsChecked: A · People and their beliefs, person/abstract noun/verb/adjective families
B · Definition of pacifism and annotated vocabulary
C · Other expressions relating to believing and context contrasts
Exercises 36.1–36.4 including the word-family table and corresponding answer-key entries

items.pt: adepto; seguidor de uma ideia ou doutrina
items.example: The movement gained adherents among younger voters.
items.note: Often adherent of a belief or group; a relatively formal term for a supporter.

items.pt: adesão; observância de princípios ou regras
items.example: The organisation insists on adherence to its ethical code.
items.note: A formal noun often followed by to; means following a belief, rule or practice.

items.pt: aderir a; seguir fielmente (uma ideia ou regra)
items.example: Members are expected to adhere to the agreed principles.
items.note: Formal verb pattern adhere to + noun; does not take a direct object without to.

items.pt: convertido; pessoa que passou a adotar uma crença
items.example: A recent convert described how her views had changed.
items.note: As a noun for a person, the usual British stress falls on the first syllable.

items.pt: converter; fazer mudar de crença; converter-se
items.example: He eventually converted to the new faith.
items.note: Verb stress usually falls on the second syllable; convert to a religion is a common pattern.

items.pt: conversão; mudança de crença ou convicção
items.example: Her conversion surprised people who had known her for years.
items.note: A noun for the process or result of changing convictions, not the person.

items.example: Critics dismissed the activist as a fanatic rather than debating his argument.
items.note: Can be strongly disapproving when applied to beliefs or intense devotion.

items.example: The essay examines how fanaticism can undermine discussion.
items.note: The abstract noun for extreme, sometimes unreasoning devotion.

items.example: His fanatical commitment left little room for compromise.
items.note: The adjective often has a negative tone, especially with ideas or campaigns.

items.pt: radical; pessoa favorável a mudanças profundas
items.example: Several radicals argued for a complete redesign of the political system.
items.note: In the book, a person favouring extreme change, especially political.

items.example: The historian traced the rise of radicalism in the region.
items.note: Abstract noun for radical political or social views.

items.example: The study looks at factors that may radicalise isolated individuals.
items.note: British -ise spelling; describes a shift towards increasingly radical beliefs.

items.pt: reacionário; contrário a reformas e mudanças
items.example: The proposal was condemned as reactionary by its opponents.
items.note: Usually disapproving, suggesting resistance to social or political change.

items.pt: reação; resposta a uma ideia ou acontecimento
items.example: The policy provoked a strong reaction from community groups.
items.note: Word-family relation to reactionary, but reaction alone is not necessarily conservative.

items.example: The course examines pacifism as a response to armed conflict.
items.note: The view that war and violence should be rejected; different pacifist positions may vary.

items.example: The pacifist refused to support the military campaign.
items.note: A supporter of pacifism; the noun can also be used adjectivally.

items.example: Campaigners seek to reduce discrimination in public services.
items.note: Formal verb pattern seek to + infinitive; stronger in written English than try to.

items.example: The initiative aims to eradicate illiteracy in the district.
items.note: Means remove completely; stronger than reduce or limit.

items.example: The panel debated whether such restrictions were justified.
items.note: Usually involves a reason considered sufficient to defend an action.

items.example: Respect for human dignity is a key tenet of the organisation's philosophy.
items.note: Tenet is a formally held principle, commonly used of doctrines and beliefs.

items.example: A prominent proponent of the reform addressed the conference.
items.note: Formal term for someone who publicly supports a plan or belief.

items.example: Much of the practice derives from older community traditions.
items.note: The source is followed by from; useful for tracing the origins of beliefs.

items.example: The association continues to oppose violence in political disputes.
items.note: Oppose is transitive here: oppose violence, not oppose to violence.

items.example: The students considered difficult ethical questions about self-defence.
items.note: British spelling defence; legal and ethical meanings depend on context.

items.pt: fazer campanha por; mobilizar-se em defesa de
items.example: Local groups campaigned for improvements in access to education.
items.note: A sustained organised effort in support of a cause or change.

items.example: The campaign used civil disobedience to challenge the legislation.
items.note: A form of protest involving deliberate refusal to obey particular laws or rules.

items.example: The protesters adopted peaceful resistance rather than armed action.
items.note: A collocation for non-violent opposition; not a guarantee that authorities will respond peacefully.

items.example: She gradually adopted a belief in non-violent conflict resolution.
items.note: Adopt can mean accept an idea as one's own; unlike inherit, it implies taking it on.

items.example: Her viewpoint changed after she heard the witnesses.
items.note: Largely equivalent to point of view when describing a person's position.

items.example: The report considers the problem from several points of view.
items.note: A standard expression for a perspective or judgement; also used in narrative analysis.

items.example: The witness gave a credible explanation of the delay.
items.note: Something credible can reasonably be believed; it need not be fully proven.

items.example: The story sounded incredible, but the documents supported it.
items.note: Can mean hard to believe or, in positive informal use, exceptionally good.

items.example: She looked incredulous when she heard the unexpected result.
items.note: Typically describes a person or reaction, unlike credible, which describes something believable.

items.example: The scam targeted gullible customers with unrealistic promises.
items.note: Disapproving: too ready to believe or trust misleading claims.

items.example: Assessing artistic originality inevitably involves subjective judgement.
items.note: Influenced by feelings or opinions; not automatically invalid, but distinct from objective.

items.example: The committee used objective criteria to evaluate each application.
items.note: Here an adjective contrasting with subjective; as a noun it can also mean goal.

items.example: Her explanation was plausible even before the records were checked.
items.note: A claim can sound reasonable without being demonstrated to be true.

items.example: The proposed timeline seemed implausible to the investigators.
items.note: Unlikely to be true or convincing; the ordinary opposite of plausible.

items.pt: atribuir algo a alguém ou a uma causa
items.example: Researchers attribute the improvement to changes in the procedure.
items.note: The pattern is attribute something to someone or something; not prove beyond doubt.
items.speechText: attribute the outcome to the new policy

items.example: I presume the organisers will send the details shortly.
items.note: An assumption treated as likely without complete certainty.

items.example: A defendant must be presumed innocent until proven guilty.
items.note: A formal legal collocation used in the exercises.

items.word: give someone the benefit of the doubt
items.pt: conceder o benefício da dúvida a alguém
items.example: Without clear evidence, the manager gave her the benefit of the doubt.
items.note: Accept someone's account provisionally despite uncertainty; a fixed idiom.
items.speechText: give her the benefit of the doubt

items.word: take something with a pinch of salt
items.pt: desconfiar de algo; não acreditar inteiramente
items.example: I take the company's impressive sales predictions with a pinch of salt.
items.note: British idiom meaning treat a statement sceptically; US usage often has grain of salt.
items.speechText: take that with a pinch of salt

items.example: Several unsigned drawings are attributed to the same artist.
items.note: A common passive construction for claims about authorship or origin.
